skeleton:
Air-Fryer Full English Breakfast

British · Easy · Serves 2

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The full English, rebuilt around the one machine half the nation now owns. Done right — and the rightness is entirely in the staging — an air fryer produces a genuinely proper fry-up: bacon that stays flat and crisps like it came off a café griddle, sausages that burst with snap, black pudding with a sealed crust, hash browns that shed their greasiness, and tomatoes that blister and slump. The eggs, alone, are better made in a pan; the air fryer's dry heat is a poor egg-cooker, and this recipe is honest about that. The doctrine is this: the air fryer is a small convection oven with a fan's worth of attitude, and a full English is a parade of components with different cooking times. So this runs as a staged sequence, not a single basket-dump — longest cooks first, a quick toss between stages, and everything landing inside 25 minutes with about 4 minutes of actual work.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The meats

The vegetables and potato

The eggs and bread (pan-finished)

Seasoning

- **Know your machine.** Air fryers run 5–20 °C hotter than their setting suggests and basket sizes vary from 2 to 8 litres. The times below assume a 4–5 litre basket at a genuine 190 °C; if yours runs fierce, drop 10 °C or pull 2 minutes early at every stage. The first cook is a calibration. - **Prick the sausages once** with a pin — once, not repeatedly. A single pinhole vents the steam that would otherwise split the skin; a dozen holes drain the juiciness out. - **Nothing stacked, nothing overlapping.** Air must circle each piece or it steams. If your basket crowds, cook the bacon in two stages or accept a two-person, 30-minute breakfast. - Set the fried-egg pan and butter by the hob for the final 4 minutes — the air fryer handles everything except the eggs.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Sausages: 12 minutes, browned, once-pricked, juices clear.
  • Bacon: flat, glassy-crisp fat, rosy eye; pulled at 6 of the 8 minutes.
  • Black pudding: crusted and holding; hash browns: deep gold, lacy edges.
  • Eggs: pan-fried and butter-basted, yolks running; plate assembled hot and simultaneous.

Air-Fryer Full English Breakfast

Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 25 minutes · Total: 35 minutes · Serves 2

Ingredients

The meats

  • 4 rashers (about 200 g) smoked back bacon
  • 4 pork sausages (about 320 g), pricked once each
  • 4 thick slices (200 g) black pudding

The vegetables and potato

  • 2 medium vine tomatoes (200 g), halved through the equator
  • 150 g chestnut mushrooms, halved if large
  • 2 frozen hash browns (about 180 g), or the homemade ones, par-frozen
  • 1 tsp (5 ml) olive oil, for the mushrooms and tomatoes

The eggs and bread (pan-finished)

  • 4 large eggs (220 g)
  • 15 g butter
  • 2 slices (100 g) thick white bread, or fried bread's civilian cousin

Seasoning

  • 3 g fine sea salt
  • 1 g black pepper
  • 1 tsp (3 g) brown sugar, for the tomatoes
  • Brown breakfast sauce, to serve

Instructions

  1. **Sausages first — 12 minutes at 190 °C.** Lay the pricked sausages in the basket with space between them. Air fry 12 minutes, turning once at 6 minutes, until deep golden-brown with taut, glossy skins. Checkpoint — the skins are evenly browned and tight, the ends have split slightly at the pinhole, and a sausage cut across shows cooked, juicy, not-pink meat with clear juices running.
  2. **Add the bacon and black pudding — 8 minutes more.** At the sausages' 12-minute mark, rest the bacon rashers on top of the sausages (their fat bastes as it renders) and lay the black pudding slices beside them. Continue at 190 °C for 8 minutes, pulling the bacon out at 6 minutes — it finishes before the rest. Checkpoint — the bacon has rendered flat, its fat is crisp-edged and glassy, and the meaty eye stays rosy and just-set. The black pudding slices are crusted dark on their faces, holding their shape, with the fat beading at their surfaces — no crumbly collapse.
  3. **Hash browns and tomatoes — the parallel stage.** If your basket is roomy, nestle the hash browns and tomato halves (cut-face up, sprinkled with the sugar, salt, and a drop of oil each) among the sausages for the final 6–8 minutes. If not, pull the cooked meats to a covered plate, drop the temperature to 200 °C, and give the hash browns 8 minutes and the tomatoes 6, together. Checkpoint — the hash browns are deeply golden on both faces with lacy browned edges and no pale, steamy spots. The tomatoes have slumped, their cut faces blistered and jammy, their juices bubbled down to a glaze in the cavity.
  4. **Mushrooms — the last 5 minutes.** Toss the mushrooms with the teaspoon of oil and a pinch of salt, add them for the final 5 minutes of whichever stage is running, and shake the basket once halfway. Checkpoint — the mushrooms are browned and glossy, shrunk by a third, with no grey watery look — the fan has done the dry-then-fat browning in reverse, which suits the machine.
  5. **The eggs, in the pan, while everything rests.** Melt the butter in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the 4 eggs to the butter-basted master's spec — 2–3 minutes, basting, yolks runny. Toast or pan-fry the bread in the leftover butter. Checkpoint — whites set, yolks liquid, lacy fringes where the butter worked — the pan's contribution, 4 minutes, the one the machine cannot make.
  6. **Assemble at once.** Everything lands on two warm plates: sausage, bacon, black pudding, hash brown, tomato, mushrooms, egg, toast, and the brown sauce on the side. Checkpoint — the plate test: every component hot at the same moment, the bacon still crackling, the yolk still running when cut — the synchronous landing that staging built.

Finish & Plate

Two plates, clockwise from twelve: egg at the crown, bacon and sausage flanking, black pudding and hash brown at three and nine, tomato and mushrooms at six, toast under the egg's corner, sauce in its dish. A mug of builder's tea alongside. The air fryer's particular virtue — everything rendered of its excess fat but nothing greasy — makes this the lighter weekday version of the classic; the weekend version still belongs to the pan.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Bacon steamed grey, never crispOverlapped rashers or machine runs coolSpace the rashers; add 2 minutes; verify with an oven thermometer once
Sausages split and leakedPricked a dozen times, or too hotOne pin-prick; 190 °C, not 210 °C
Black pudding crumbled to rubbleThin slices or overcookedSlice 1.5 cm thick; pull with the bacon
Hash browns pale and softCrowded, or added cold from frozen in a cool basketPreheat 2 minutes; room for air around each
Everything done at different timesStaging ignoredLongest first, pull-and-rest to a covered plate — the sequence is the recipe

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Make-ahead:** the meats, tomatoes, and hash browns reheat well together at 180 °C for 5–6 minutes; the eggs are always cooked fresh. Cooked components keep 3 days refrigerated. - **Variation — the 15-minute weekday half:** sausages (10 minutes), bacon (6, stacked on top for the last 6), halved tomato; skip the rest, one egg in the pan. The full architecture in miniature. - **Variation — vegetarian:** swap in vegetarian sausages (10 minutes at 190 °C), keep everything else; the black pudding's slot goes to a grilled portobello cap. - **Calibration note:** after one breakfast, write your machine's true temperatures on a note stuck to its lid — every recipe thereafter, including this one, sharpens overnight.
